title: America Needs an Off-Ramp Between Doing Nothing and Shutting AI Down
gist: For 18 days in June 2026 the Commerce Department's deemed-export order forced Anthropic to shut down its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models worldwide, triggered by an Amazon jailbreak claim relayed CEO-to-cabinet-secretary with no independent validation. The author argues the United States has no standardized process or proportionate remedy ladder for frontier-model security risk, and proposes a statutory review agency built on NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation with 30-day pre-release reviews, 72-hour emergency triage, judicial review, ~$100 million annual funding and allied mutual recognition.

insights.claim: For 18 days in June 2026 two of America's most capable AI models went dark worldwide because the US government ordered it, not for technical or business reasons, with public access to Anthropic's Fable 5 restored on June 30.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Establishes regulatory shutdown as a realized, not hypothetical, tail risk for frontier AI revenue and for every application built on a single model provider.
insights.locator: For 18 days in June

insights.claim: On June 12, 2026 Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick sent Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei a letter requiring a license to provide Fable 5 and Mythos 5 to any "foreign person" worldwide, a restriction that extended even to Anthropic's own employees, so the company concluded compliance meant shutting the models down for everyone.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Deemed-export logic applied to model access can force a total global outage rather than a geographic carve-out, which makes the downside of such orders discontinuous.
insights.locator: An Unprecedented Shutdown

insights.claim: The order capped a roughly 24-hour scramble that began when Amazon security researchers reportedly found a way to jailbreak the models' guardrails and CEO Andy Jassy relayed the findings to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, meaning a competitor's private, unvalidated report drove a worldwide shutdown.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Rivals now have a demonstrated, low-cost channel to impose existential operational risk on a competitor, a governance risk factor for every frontier AI investment.
insights.locator: On Friday afternoon, June 12

insights.claim: According to Anthropic's own statement, the Commerce Secretary's letter did not explain the underlying national security concern, and it remains unclear whether any third party validated the technical claims or whether Anthropic was given sufficient recourse.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Absence of a written, reviewable determination means affected companies cannot remediate or litigate quickly, extending outage duration and uncertainty.
insights.quote: did not provide specific details of its national security concern
insights.locator: Much remains unclear

insights.claim: The shutdown followed months of open hostility: in March the Pentagon labeled Anthropic a supply chain risk after the company sought limits on how its models would be used, Pentagon research and engineering official Emil Michael publicly called Amodei a liar with a god-complex, and Pete Hegseth announced that companies using Anthropic models could no longer do business with the department.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Usage-restriction policies now carry direct commercial penalties in defense procurement, creating a measurable revenue cost to safety positioning.
insights.locator: None of this took place in a political vacuum

insights.claim: An administration that is resoundingly against AI regulation in word and deed nonetheless imposed the most restrictive action in the history of American AI policy, showing that the absence of institutions produces arbitrary intervention rather than less intervention.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Deregulatory rhetoric is not a reliable predictor of low regulatory risk in AI; process design matters more than stated policy stance.
insights.quote: An administration resoundingly against AI regulation in word and deed had effectively banned two of America’s most capable AI models worldwide.
insights.locator: An Unprecedented Shutdown

themes.theme: Legal fragility of executive AI restrictions

insights.claim: Whether the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 and its deemed-export rules even apply to a foreign person's access to a hosted American AI model is unsettled, because as a Harvard Law Review analysis observes, when a foreign national prompts a model on American servers the software never leaves the country.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: The legal foundation of model-access export controls is weak, so similar orders are vulnerable to being vacated, adding volatility rather than durable restriction.
insights.locator: Shaky Legal Ground

insights.claim: On June 23 Legion LegalTech, an Anthropic customer, sued arguing the directive "exceeds every source of statutory authority on which it could conceivably rest," including the International Emergency Economic Powers Act whose Berman Amendment excludes informational materials.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Downstream customers, not just model developers, are now the plaintiffs, which broadens the litigation surface around AI export actions.
insights.quote: exceeds every source of statutory authority on which it could conceivably rest
insights.locator: The first legal challenge arrived on June 23

insights.claim: Legion's most consequential argument invokes the major questions doctrine, central to the Supreme Court's February decision striking down the administration's emergency-powers tariffs, implying that only clear congressional authorization can give executive AI regulation durable legal footing.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: If courts extend the tariff precedent to AI, unilateral executive model restrictions become legally fragile, shifting the locus of AI regulatory risk to Congress.
insights.locator: Most consequentially, Legion invokes the major questions doctrine

insights.claim: Creating an evaluator and creating the legal authority to act on its findings are two separate problems: an agency without substantive authority leaves government reaching for ill-fitting emergency tools, while authority without a credible evaluator produces remedies untethered from validated findings.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: A diagnostic for judging any proposed AI governance reform: legislation that supplies only one half will reproduce the June outcome.
insights.locator: These legal questions expose a distinction

insights.claim: Any workable regime must keep the burden of proof on the government, with no restriction persisting absent an independently validated finding and a written determination, and orders lapsing automatically if deadlines pass unmet.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Automatic sunset on unsubstantiated orders would cap the duration of outages like the 18-day shutdown, materially reducing commercial risk.
insights.locator: Throughout, the burden of proof rests with the government

insights.claim: Congress should create a statutory AI security review agency using the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, housed within NIST, as its technical backbone, granting statutory independence and protected funding to fast-track creation.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
entities: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
insights.so_what: CAISI is the likely institutional vehicle for any US frontier-model gate, so its funding and authorities are the thing to track for compliance-cost forecasting.
insights.locator: The Case for a Statutory Review Agency

insights.claim: The proposed process standard is a 30-day pre-release review with third-party validation and written findings, plus authority for a 72-hour emergency review followed by a temporary mitigation order, independent validation and a mandatory written determination within 30 days.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
entities: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
insights.so_what: A concrete timetable model labs would have to build into release planning, and a known, priceable cost compared with unbounded ad hoc shutdowns.
insights.locator: The standard should be a 30-day pre-release review

insights.claim: The remedy regime should be a proportionality ladder rather than a binary approve-or-pull choice: a narrow jailbreak requires a patch and monitoring, moderate misuse uplift means conditional deployment with narrower access and enhanced logging, bypassable safeguards on high-risk capability means temporary restrictions and controlled access, and only an acute national security threat triggers an emergency order and classified review.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: The single most transferable idea in the piece: had this ladder existed in June, the government would have had options between doing nothing and switching off two models globally.
insights.locator: The regime should be proportionate

insights.claim: A 72-hour emergency review is feasible because it is claim triage rather than a de novo evaluation, validating a specific exploit claim against baselines the agency already holds from a standing pre-release process.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
entities: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
insights.so_what: Answers the main technical objection to fast regulatory review, meaning speed is not a credible argument against building the institution.
insights.locator: Skeptics will ask how anyone conducts a credible frontier-model review in 72 hours

insights.claim: The Center for AI Standards and Innovation has already conducted more than 40 evaluations and holds pre-deployment agreements with Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
entities: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
insights.so_what: The pre-deployment access relationships already exist, so a mandatory gate would formalize current practice rather than build from scratch.
insights.locator: There is evidence this works

insights.claim: The same review process should apply to OpenAI, Google, xAI, Amazon, Meta and any other developer whose frontier model raises comparable national security questions, rather than being an argument for adopting any single company's preferred policy position.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Signals that compliance burden would fall across all frontier labs, converting a firm-specific shock into an industry-wide, priceable cost.
insights.locator: This is not an argument for adopting Anthropic's preferred policy position

insights.claim: American AI offerings already cost more than less advanced but capable Chinese alternatives, so when Chinese models are near-frontier, cheaper and increasingly easy to deploy, every unpredictable pause in US access risks pushing developers, enterprises and governments toward a rival stack.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Regulatory outages are a share-shift catalyst toward Chinese model providers, so shutdown events should be watched as competitive-position data, not just legal news.
insights.locator: This matters well beyond Anthropic

insights.claim: The diffusion of AI is at least as important to US competitiveness as staying at the technological cutting edge, so unilateral restrictions smooth the path for Chinese firms to gain market share and standard-setting influence.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Reframes AI competition from benchmark leadership to installed base, which favors distribution, pricing and reliability over headline capability.
insights.locator: This matters because the diffusion of AI

insights.claim: Other American frontier companies are close to developing capabilities on par with Mythos 5 and Chinese AI companies may not be far behind, given how much the model performance gap has closed.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Capability parity across multiple vendors erodes any single lab's pricing power and makes model-agnostic architectures the rational customer choice.
insights.locator: Other American frontier companies are close

insights.claim: The June shutdown cut off every downstream customer mid-deployment worldwide for 18 days, and Legion told the court that losing access was eroding its viability as a business.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Single-model dependency is now a demonstrated existential risk for AI-native companies, which strengthens the case for multi-model abstraction layers and routing tools.
insights.locator: The June shutdown cut off every downstream customer

insights.claim: A June 2 executive order directed agencies to develop classified benchmarking and a voluntary framework for evaluating frontier models up to 30 days before release while explicitly disclaiming any mandatory licensing, preclearance or permitting regime, and ten days later the same administration imposed the most restrictive action in American AI policy history.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Direct evidence that voluntary frameworks do not prevent emergency intervention, so companies should not treat voluntary regimes as regulatory safe harbor.
insights.locator: A June 2 executive order directed agencies

insights.claim: National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said in May that the White House was studying an executive order establishing a pre-release security review, likening it to the Food and Drug Administration's drug approval process.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: An FDA-style gate for frontier models is already under internal consideration, which would lengthen release cycles and advantage labs with regulatory affairs capacity.
insights.locator: National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said in May

insights.claim: A mandatory 30-day pre-release gate is the lesser burden than ad hoc shutdowns because it would run largely in parallel with red-teaming labs already conduct, it is a known and priceable cost, and certification can become a market asset the way FedRAMP accelerated federal cloud adoption through a reusable security authorization baseline.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Points to a compliance moat: a rigorous US security certification would function as a procurement advantage abroad, favoring incumbents that can absorb the process.
insights.locator: A mandatory pre-release gate might seem to damage diffusion

insights.claim: The status quo, not a statutory agency, is the capture scenario: the June shutdown was set in motion by a competitor's private report to a cabinet secretary, adjudicated behind closed doors, with no independent validation and no public written record, so outcomes turn on which chief executive has which secretary's cell phone number.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Inverts the standard libertarian objection to AI regulators, and identifies political access as the currently decisive competitive variable in US AI policy.
insights.locator: Designing Against Capture, and Paying for It

insights.claim: Anti-capture design should be engineered into statute through fixed staggered leadership terms, mandatory unclassified findings, conflict-of-interest and cooling-off rules, multiple competing accredited evaluators, funding by appropriations rather than industry fees, and Government Accountability Office review with a reauthorization sunset.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: A checklist for judging whether any actual AI agency bill is credible or is industry-funded capture in disguise.
insights.locator: Resistance should still be engineered into the statute

insights.claim: The Center for AI Standards and Innovation cannot do this job today with roughly 30 staff and about $30 million in total funding since 2024, roughly one-tenth of what its British counterpart spends, while the Institute for Progress puts an equipped version at about $84 million per year and other frameworks propose $100 million per year.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
entities: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
insights.so_what: The cost of a credible US frontier-model regulator is trivial relative to the stakes, on the order of a single F-35, so funding is a political choice rather than a fiscal constraint.
insights.quote: This is trivial given the stakes, on the order of a single F-35.
insights.locator: Resourcing is where proposals like this go to die

insights.claim: Even the administration-aligned America First Policy Institute describes the Center for AI Standards and Innovation as "chronically underfunded," indicating cross-ideological agreement on the resourcing gap.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
entities: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
insights.so_what: Bipartisan-adjacent consensus on funding raises the probability that CAISI appropriations increase even without a new statute.
insights.locator: Even the administration-aligned America First Policy Institute

insights.claim: To staff a real review function the new agency would need excepted service pay, detailees from the National Security Agency and the national laboratories, and a classified compute enclave.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
entities: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
insights.so_what: Cleared talent and classified compute are the binding constraints on government AI evaluation capacity, an underappreciated procurement opportunity.
insights.locator: The new agency should permit excepted service pay

insights.claim: Critics in the frontier AI safety community are right that the Center for AI Standards and Innovation is too politicized to serve as a credible regulator today, because its remit has shifted with the administration and its leadership serves at the pleasure of the commerce secretary, but that is an argument for a statute rather than against an agency.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
entities: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
insights.so_what: Distinguishes institutional design failure from institutional impossibility, which is the crux of whether US AI governance stabilizes.
insights.locator: Many in the frontier AI safety community counter

insights.claim: Allies are already routing around the United States because American export control decisions have become unpredictable and are increasingly perceived as weaponized, so a statutory, transparent, court-reviewable process would help restore allied confidence in US leadership.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Allied hedging against US tech dependence is a structural trend that creates demand for non-American AI and semiconductor supply options.
insights.locator: The Allied Play

insights.claim: Allies have affirmative reasons to join a US review regime: the frontier models they deploy are overwhelmingly American, most allied bodies do measurement science and lack the model access, compute and cleared talent for frontier reviews, and mutual recognition would spare their companies duplicative compliance across fragmented national gates that would otherwise cede standard-setting influence to Beijing.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Fragmented national AI approval gates are the main compliance-cost risk for multinational AI deployment, so mutual recognition progress is a margin story.
insights.locator: Allies also have affirmative reasons to join

insights.claim: The proposed vehicle is the Center for AI Standards and Innovation's International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation, and Science with its 10 member governments, expanded to add India, Israel, the Netherlands and Taiwan for their semiconductor weight and growing AI capability.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
entities: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
insights.so_what: Names the specific jurisdictions likely to be pulled into AI evaluation governance, which tends to precede coordinated export-control alignment affecting semiconductor supply chains.
insights.locator: The Center for AI Standards and Innovation's International Network

insights.claim: The sequencing for allied cooperation should be mutual recognition of security evaluations first, common test standards second, and export control alignment only as the long-term horizon.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Gives a staged timeline for watching whether allied AI governance converges, with export-control harmonization the last and least likely step.
insights.locator: The sequencing matters

insights.claim: The United States cannot lead global AI development and diffusion if its own companies and allies cannot predict how security decisions will be made, so predictability itself is a competitive advantage and leaving the current approach unaddressed risks ceding AI leadership to China.
insights.speaker: Martijn Rasser
insights.so_what: Frames regulatory predictability, not looser rules, as the variable that determines whether the American AI stack keeps global customers.
insights.locator: Predictability Is Power

top_entities: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
